=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003), Paperbark Analytics, AUD 24m, debt-free/cash-free, NSW law

---

## 1. Threshold point: the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing

The Seller's preamble says these positions were "settled at principal level by both deal teams," are "FINAL," and reflect "standard and widely accepted market terms." **This is the Seller's characterisation, not an agreed fact.** Nothing in the materials shows a buyer-side sign-off.

- **Action:** Please confirm internally whether any Wattlebridge principal agreed to any of these points. Unless someone did, treat every position below as open.
- Some "market" claims are defensible as general cap and basket ranges. Others are not market for a buyer, including fundamental warranties under the general cap, the general data-room disclosure, constructive buyer knowledge, and limitations applying to fraud.
- **The Seller's own documents contradict each other.** The Update says Bluefen is "addressed" and DD-006 is "not material." The Disclosure Letter says no Bluefen consent exists and the incident investigation is preliminary, with scope and notification unresolved. We should rely on the Disclosure Letter's factual statements and reject the Update's characterisations.

---

## 2. Value at risk

| Item | Amount (AUD) | Seller's position | Our view |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~3,200,000 | Release *after* Completion | Must be repaid and released **at** Completion from the price |
| DD-005 bonuses | 420,000 + on-costs | "Matter for the Seller," not in funds flow | Debt-like item, deducted from price |
| Ironquay SOW3 | 180,000 (+ IP risk) | Indemnity limited to the payment | Pay or deduct, take an assignment, and get a broader indemnity |
| Sandbar renewals | 330,000 | "Ordinary course" | Unverified. Possibly leakage or a debt-like item |
| Bluefen revenue | ~3,600,000 p.a. (~30%) | "Addressed" | Unconditional consent required as a condition precedent |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified | "Not material" | Specific indemnity plus retention |

Riverlark, the bonuses, Ironquay and Sandbar together come to about **AUD 4.13m (~17% of price)**. That is before on-costs, Bluefen revenue risk and any privacy exposure. On the Seller's drafting, much of this would fall to the Buyer or sit behind the cap, basket and knowledge exclusions.

---

## 3. Issue-by-issue analysis

### A. Liability architecture

**3.1 General cap (cl 12.1): 20% / AUD 4.8m**
- The figure is negotiable for general warranties. If we take W&I insurance, 20% or less may be acceptable with the policy sitting above it. Without W&I, push for 30–50%.
- **The real issue is scope.** The cap must not apply to fundamental warranties (title and capacity), tax, specific indemnities, covenant or leakage claims, price adjustments, or fraud. Those should be capped at 100% of price, or uncapped for fraud.

**3.2 Thresholds (cl 12.2): de minimis AUD 25k; basket AUD 250k, recovering only the excess**
- A basket of about 1.04% of price is within range, but a **deductible basket is seller-friendly.** Push for a **tipping basket** so that once the threshold is reached, recovery runs from the first dollar.
- Lower the de minimis to around AUD 10k. Add an aggregation rule so that related or similar claims from the same facts count together. This matters for the three linked Sandbar renewals and any multi-record privacy claims.
- Thresholds must not apply to fundamental, tax, indemnity, leakage or fraud claims.

**3.3 Time limits (cl 12.3/13): 18 months; the limitation applies "to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"**
- 18 months for general warranties is arguable. Ask for 24 months, so that at least two audit cycles fall within it.
- **Reject the "all Claims" default.** It reverses the burden: anything we fail to carve out expressly gets an 18-month limit. The default should run the other way, with the 18-month limit applying only to general Warranty Claims.
- Tax: the period should track ATO amendment periods plus a buffer (commonly 5–7 years), with no limit for fraud or evasion.
- Title and capacity: 6–7 years, or the statutory limitation period.
- Specific indemnities: tailored periods. For DD-006, at least until regulatory and third-party exposure has run its course.

**3.4 Fundamental warranties under general caps "for administrative simplicity"**
- **Reject outright.** If title fails, we have paid AUD 24m for shares we do not own. A 20% cap and an 18-month window would leave 80% of the price unprotected. Title and capacity must be capped at 100% of price, sit outside thresholds, and run for a long limitation period. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to accept this.

**3.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying "to all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)**
- **Reject.** As drafted, this would arguably limit claims for **fraud, dishonest concealment and wilful misconduct.** Insert an express carve-out for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller and its representatives, including the knowledge of management.
- Also carve out specific indemnities, covenants (including the pre-Completion conduct and leakage covenants), price adjustment and completion-accounts mechanics, and title.
- Note for NSW and Australian law: claims under ACL s18 (misleading or deceptive conduct) cannot simply be contracted out of. Non-reliance clauses can still be used evidentially against a buyer, so we should resist broad non-reliance wording rather than depend on that protection. *Confirm with NSW litigation counsel.*

### B. Disclosure and knowledge

**3.6 General disclosure of the data room and public registers (DL 1.1–1.2)**

This is one of the most damaging provisions in the package. It would qualify every warranty by everything in DD-002 to DD-012, the Accounts, the statutory registers and all public records.
- **Push for specific disclosure only.** Disclosures should qualify warranties only where they are made against specific warranties, fairly, and with enough detail for the Buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Reject general data-room disclosure. If that is commercially impossible, accept it only for documents expressly listed in an agreed index, with a "fairly disclosed" standard.
- Delete the words **"or referred to in."** They would sweep in documents that are referenced but not actually in the data room.
- Delete the disclosure of "publicly searchable corporate records" as a general matter, or limit it to searches the Buyer actually ran on specified dates.
- Require the data room index to be annexed and an archive copy to be delivered on USB or by escrow.
- **Staleness:** the data room cut-off is 22 September 2026, and it is now 5 November. Any **bring-down or supplementary disclosure** before Completion must not cure warranty breaches. It should instead give the Buyer a termination right or an indemnity.
- DL 1.4 (non-admission) is common and broadly acceptable. It must not undercut the specific indemnities.

**3.7 Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3)**

The Seller's wording covers knowledge of "the Buyer or its advisers," including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is constructive knowledge on top of general disclosure, and together they would remove almost all protection.
- Our best position is a **pro-sandbagging** clause: Buyer knowledge does not affect claims.
- Our fallback is **actual** knowledge of a small number of named Wattlebridge individuals, excluding advisers, excluding constructive or imputed knowledge, and excluding anything "discoverable."
- This matters most because **we already know about Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar.** Under any knowledge exclusion, warranty claims on these would fail. **Every known issue therefore needs a specific indemnity, a condition precedent, or a price deduction. Warranties alone will not protect us.**

### C. Specific matters

**3.8 Bluefen change of control (cl 3/6.3; DL 2; DD-002 cl 11.2/11.3)**

Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m in FY26 revenue (~30%). The Disclosure Letter confirms that no consent has been obtained and that the cl 11.3 conditions have not been shown to be satisfied.

The Seller's mechanism has two problems:
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation.
- "Satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. A consent given subject to conditions, such as repricing, new terms or a shortened term, would count as satisfying the condition.

Our position:
- An **unconditional** written consent and waiver from Bluefen, or one given only on conditions acceptable to the Buyer in its absolute discretion, should be a condition precedent to Completion.
- Any cl 11.3 conditions must be satisfied, with evidence.
- The Buyer alone can waive the condition. The Seller should have a **best endeavours** obligation, the Buyer should have the right to participate in the approach to Bluefen, and the Buyer should be able to walk away at the sunset date.
- Consider a price adjustment or retention if Bluefen gives notice or reduces volume within 12 months after Completion.
- Check DD-002 for any termination-for-convenience right. If one exists, a consent alone may not protect the revenue.

**3.9 Riverlark facility (cl 2/7; DL 3; DD-003 cl 8.1/9.2)**

About AUD 3.2m is outstanding, there is a change-of-control trigger, and the facility has not been repaid. A "release to be provided following Completion" is **inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free.** It also risks Completion itself causing an event of default under cl 8.1 while the security remains over the Company.

Our position:
- A payoff letter from Riverlark before Completion confirming the exact payoff amount, including break costs, accrued interest and fees.
- Repayment from the purchase price at Completion through the funds flow, treated as Debt.
- A deed of release, PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to lodge them within one business day), and the return of title documents, all delivered **at** Completion.
- No reliance on a post-Completion release.

**3.10 Employee completion bonuses (DD-005; DL 5): AUD 420,000**

"A matter for the Seller" is meaningless unless it is built into the price. The bonuses are payable by the Company, are triggered by the sale, and are not in the funds flow.
- Treat them as **Debt or a transaction expense, deducted from the price.** This should include PAYG withholding, payroll tax, superannuation where applicable (SG treatment depends on whether the bonus is OTE, so tax advisers should confirm), workers' compensation and other on-costs.
- Where the bonuses depend on post-Completion continued employment, still deduct them, or hold the amount in escrow and release unearned portions to the Seller.
- Add an indemnity for any other change-of-control or retention payments not disclosed.

**3.11 Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DL 4; DD-004 cl 7.3; DD-010)**

Transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on **cleared payment of every SOW3 fee.** At least AUD 180,000 appears to be unpaid, and there is no confirmatory assignment. Until both happen, the Company may not own IP that could be core to the SaaS product.

An indemnity limited to "the specific SOW3 payment" does not cover the real risk: loss of ownership, infringement claims, the cost of re-developing or licensing the IP, and customer claims.

Our position:
- Confirm whether "every SOW3 fee" is limited to the AUD 180,000, or whether milestones, variations or disputed amounts are also outstanding.
- Require payment by the Seller before Completion, or deduction from the price and payment directly to Ironquay through the funds flow.
- A **confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay**, with moral rights consents where relevant, as a Completion deliverable or condition precedent.
- A broad specific indemnity covering any loss from the Company's failure to own or have the right to use the SOW3 materials. It should sit outside the general cap and thresholds, be unaffected by disclosure or knowledge, and have a long claim period.
- Check whether the Ironquay materials are embedded in the current product. The commercial and DD teams should map this.

**3.12 Export / privacy incident (cl 4.6/Sch 6; DL 6; DD-006)**

A download link to an export of about 1,240 records was sent to an unintended external address. The records include names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. Whether the file was accessed, the exact scope, and whether notification is required are all unknown. Calling this "not expected to be material" is not supported by the Seller's own disclosure.

The **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme** (Privacy Act 1988 Part IIIC) requires an assessment of a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days where reasonably practicable. The incident predates 22 September. If no assessment has been completed, there may already be a **compliance issue**, separate from whether the breach is notifiable. Penalties for serious interferences with privacy have increased materially in recent years, and customer contracts may contain their own notification and indemnity obligations. *Confirm current thresholds and timing with privacy counsel.*

Our position:
- **Before Completion:** the full incident file, any forensic report, the NDB assessment and the decision record, and confirmation of whether OAIC and individuals have been notified. Also check customer contracts for breach notification obligations.
- A **specific indemnity** covering regulatory investigation costs, notification and remediation costs, and third-party, customer and individual claims. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds, be unaffected by disclosure or knowledge, and have a claim period of at least 3–4 years. Note that indemnities for civil penalties may face public policy limits. Recovery of associated costs is more secure, so pair the indemnity with a **retention or escrow.**
- Warranties that, apart from DD-006, there have been no other incidents, and that the Company complies with its privacy obligations.

**3.13 Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008/DD-011; DL 8): 3 × AUD 110,000**

The Seller asserts these are "ordinary course" without evidence. The Disclosure Letter does not say whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course. The three renewals are described as "related," and splitting into three may keep each below internal approval thresholds.

Questions to put to the Seller:
- Is Sandbar related to Harbourglass?
- When were the renewals signed relative to the sale process?
- What are the term and termination rights?
- Is this a duplication or an increase over prior spend?

Our position:
- If Sandbar is Seller-related, treat the renewals as **leakage** (locked box) or as a debt-like or working capital adjustment.
- If they were entered after the sale process began, they should have needed Buyer consent under the pre-Completion conduct covenants.
- Otherwise, require a specific indemnity or price reduction for any amount not commercially justified.

**3.14 Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"**

Reject this.
- **Tax:** a standalone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, including tax on the bonuses and any payroll tax or super shortfall. It should be capped at 100% of price, sit outside thresholds, and run for the tax limitation periods described above.
- **IP:** for a SaaS target, IP ownership and non-infringement warranties should at least have a higher cap and a longer period than general warranties. The Ironquay issue shows why.

**3.15 Title (DD-012; DL 10)**

The share register alone is not sufficient evidence of title. The Disclosure Letter itself notes that it "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification."

Our position:
- Title warranties as fundamental warranties (see 3.4), covering no encumbrances, options or other rights over shares.
- Verify against ASIC records, the constitution, any shareholders' agreement (pre-emption waivers), PPSR searches against the Company and the Seller, and historical share issue and transfer documentation.
- Completion deliverables: signed share transfer forms, share certificates (or lost certificate indemnities), board approvals, waivers, director resignations and releases.

**3.16 Office lease (DD-007; DL 7) and Mossvale (DD-009; DL 9)**

These are likely lower risk, but both Disclosure Letter statements are carefully worded ("does not describe it as…," "does not state…"). We should verify them ourselves.
- Confirm that the lease requires notification only and not consent. Put the notice into the completion steps.
- Confirm that the Mossvale restriction on assignment has no change-of-control or deemed-assignment limb.

---

## 4. Recommendations summary

**Reject outright**
1. Title and capacity warranties under the general cap and time limits. These must be capped at 100% of price, sit outside thresholds, and run for 6–7 years.
2. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature." Carve out fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, indemnities, covenants, leakage and price mechanics.
3. The "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated" default.
4. Constructive, adviser or "discoverable" buyer knowledge. Seek pro-sandbagging, with a fallback to actual knowledge of named individuals.
5. General data-room and public-records disclosure. Seek specific, fair disclosure only, delete "or referred to in," and ensure no cure by bring-down disclosure.
6. The post-Completion Riverlark release.
7. The "settled" status of tax and IP under the general regime.

**Restructure as conditions precedent or Completion deliverables**
8. An unconditional Bluefen consent, with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, waivable by the Buyer only, and best endeavours on the Seller.
9. The Riverlark payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges at Completion.
10. The Ironquay confirmatory assignment, with SOW3 fees paid or deducted.
11. A complete DD-006 incident file and NDB assessment before signing or Completion.

**Price and funds flow**
12. Deduct Riverlark (full payoff amount), the bonuses plus on-costs, and any unpaid Ironquay fees as Debt. Investigate Sandbar as possible leakage or a debt-like item.
13. Add a retention or escrow sized to the DD-006 and Bluefen exposures, or obtain W&I cover with these matters handled outside the policy, since W&I will typically exclude known issues.

**Specific indemnities**, outside the cap, thresholds, disclosure and knowledge
14. DD-006 privacy incident.
15. Ironquay IP, covering ownership and infringement and not just the payment.
16. Pre-Completion tax, including on the bonuses.
17. Undisclosed change-of-control or transaction payments.
18. Sandbar, if it is not resolved through price.

**Negotiable, with suggested positions**
19. General cap: 30–50% without W&I, or around 20% plus W&I.
20. Tipping basket of about 1%. De minimis around AUD 10k with aggregation of related claims.
21. General claims period of 24 months.

**Information requests**
- Confirm internally whether any principal "settled" these points.
- Bluefen: the cl 11.3 text, any termination-for-convenience right, and the status of the approach to Bluefen.
- Riverlark: a draft payoff letter and break costs.
- Ironquay: a full SOW3 fee ledger and confirmation of what IP is embedded in the current product.
- DD-005: the bonus terms and their tax and super treatment.
- DD-006: the forensic report, NDB assessment and notifications.
- Sandbar: whether it is related to Harbourglass, contract dates, terms and termination rights.
- Title: ASIC and PPSR searches and the shareholders' agreement.
- An updated data room index, given the data room cut-off was 22 September.

*These positions should be confirmed with NSW-qualified transaction, tax and privacy counsel before the mark-up goes out. I can prepare a clause-by-clause mark-up or an issues list in the Seller's numbering if that would help.*

Non-reliance clauses can still be used evidentially against a buyer, so we should resist broad non-reliance wording rather than depend on that protection. *Confirm with NSW litigation counsel.*

### B. Disclosure and knowledge

**3.6 General disclosure of the data room and public registers (DL 1.1–1.2)**

This is one of the most damaging provisions in the package. It would qualify every warranty by everything in DD-002 to DD-012, the Accounts, the statutory registers and all public records.
- **Push for specific disclosure only.** Disclosures should qualify warranties only where they are made against specific warranties, fairly, and with enough detail for the Buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Reject general data-room disclosure. If that is commercially impossible, accept it only for documents expressly listed in an agreed index, with a "fairly disclosed" standard.
- Delete the words **"or referred to in."** They would sweep in documents that are referenced but not actually in the data room.
- Delete the disclosure of "publicly searchable corporate records" as a general matter, or limit it to searches the Buyer actually ran on specified dates.
- Require the data room index to be annexed and an archive copy to be delivered on USB or by escrow.
- **Staleness:** the data room cut-off is 22 September 2026, and it is now 5 November. Any **bring-down or supplementary disclosure** before Completion must not cure warranty breaches. It should instead give the Buyer a termination right or an indemnity.
- DL 1.4 (non-admission) is common and broadly acceptable. It must not undercut the specific indemnities.

**3.7 Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3)**

The Seller's wording covers knowledge of "the Buyer or its advisers," including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is constructive knowledge on top of general disclosure, and together they would remove almost all protection.
- Our best position is a **pro-sandbagging** clause: Buyer knowledge does not affect claims.
- Our fallback is **actual** knowledge of a small number of named Wattlebridge individuals, excluding advisers, excluding constructive or imputed knowledge, and excluding anything "discoverable."
- This matters most because **we already know about Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar.** Under any knowledge exclusion, warranty claims on these would fail. **Every known issue therefore needs a specific indemnity, a condition precedent, or a price deduction. Warranties alone will not protect us.**

### C. Specific matters

**3.8 Bluefen change of control (cl 3/6.3; DL 2; DD-002 cl 11.2/11.3)**

Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m in FY26 revenue (~30%). The Disclosure Letter confirms that no consent has been obtained and that the cl 11.3 conditions have not been shown to be satisfied.

The Seller's mechanism has two problems:
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation.
- "Satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. A consent given subject to conditions, such as repricing, new terms or a shortened term, would count as satisfying the condition.

Our position:
- An **unconditional** written consent and waiver from Bluefen, or one given only on conditions acceptable to the Buyer in its absolute discretion, should be a condition precedent to Completion.
- Any cl 11.3 conditions must be satisfied, with evidence.
- The Buyer alone can waive the condition. The Seller should have a **best endeavours** obligation, the Buyer should have the right to participate in the approach to Bluefen, and the Buyer should be able to walk away at the sunset date.
- Consider a price adjustment or retention if Bluefen gives notice or reduces volume within 12 months after Completion.
- Check DD-002 for any termination-for-convenience right. If one exists, a consent alone may not protect the revenue.

**3.9 Riverlark facility (cl 2/7; DL 3; DD-003 cl 8.1/9.2)**

About AUD 3.2m is outstanding, there is a change-of-control trigger, and the facility has not been repaid. A "release to be provided following Completion" is **inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free.** It also risks Completion itself causing an event of default under cl 8.1 while the security remains over the Company.

Our position:
- A payoff letter from Riverlark before Completion confirming the exact payoff amount, including break costs, accrued interest and fees.
- Repayment from the purchase price at Completion through the funds flow, treated as Debt.
- A deed of release, PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to lodge them within one business day), and the return of title documents, all delivered **at** Completion.
- No reliance on a post-Completion release.

**3.10 Employee completion bonuses (DD-005; DL 5): AUD 420,000**

"A matter for the Seller" is meaningless unless it is built into the price. The bonuses are payable by the Company, are triggered by the sale, and are not in the funds flow.
- Treat them as **Debt or a transaction expense, deducted from the price.** This should include PAYG withholding, payroll tax, superannuation where applicable (SG treatment depends on whether the bonus is OTE, so tax advisers should confirm), workers' compensation and other on-costs.
- Where the bonuses depend on post-Completion continued employment, still deduct them, or hold the amount in escrow and release unearned portions to the Seller.
- Add an indemnity for any other change-of-control or retention payments not disclosed.

**3.11 Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DL 4; DD-004 cl 7.3; DD-010)**

Transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on **cleared payment of every SOW3 fee.** At least AUD 180,000 appears to be unpaid, and there is no confirmatory assignment. Until both happen, the Company may not own IP that could be core to the SaaS product.

An indemnity limited to "the specific SOW3 payment" does not cover the real risk: loss of ownership, infringement claims, the cost of re-developing or licensing the IP, and customer claims.

Our position:
- Confirm whether "every SOW3 fee" is limited to the AUD 180,000, or whether milestones, variations or disputed amounts are also outstanding.
- Require payment by the Seller before Completion, or deduction from the price and payment directly to Ironquay through the funds flow.
- A **confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay**, with moral rights consents where relevant, as a Completion deliverable or condition precedent.
- A broad specific indemnity covering any loss from the Company's failure to own or have the right to use the SOW3 materials. It should sit outside the general cap and thresholds, be unaffected by disclosure or knowledge, and have a long claim period.
- Check whether the Ironquay materials are embedded in the current product. The commercial and DD teams should map this.

**3.12 Export / privacy incident (cl 4.6/Sch 6; DL 6; DD-006)**

A download link to an export of about 1,240 records was sent to an unintended external address. The records include names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. Whether the file was accessed, the exact scope, and whether notification is required are all unknown. Calling this "not expected to be material" is not supported by the Seller's own disclosure.

The **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme** (Privacy Act 1988 Part IIIC) requires an assessment of a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days where reasonably practicable. The incident predates 22 September. If no assessment has been completed, there may already be a **compliance issue**, separate from whether the breach is notifiable. Penalties for serious interferences with privacy have increased materially in recent years, and customer contracts may contain their own notification and indemnity obligations. *Confirm current thresholds and timing with privacy counsel.*

Our position:
- **Before Completion:** the full incident file, any forensic report, the NDB assessment and the decision record, and confirmation of whether OAIC and individuals have been notified. Also check customer contracts for breach notification obligations.
- A **specific indemnity** covering regulatory investigation costs, notification and remediation costs, and third-party, customer and individual claims. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds, be unaffected by disclosure or knowledge, and have a claim period of at least 3–4 years. Note that indemnities for civil penalties may face public policy limits. Recovery of associated costs is more secure, so pair the indemnity with a **retention or escrow.**
- Warranties that, apart from DD-006, there have been no other incidents, and that the Company complies with its privacy obligations.

**3.13 Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008/DD-011; DL 8): 3 × AUD 110,000**

The Seller asserts these are "ordinary course" without evidence. The Disclosure Letter does not say whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course. The three renewals are described as "related," and splitting into three may keep each below internal approval thresholds.

Questions to put to the Seller:
- Is Sandbar related to Harbourglass?
- When were the renewals signed relative to the sale process?
- What are the term and termination rights?
- Is this a duplication or an increase over prior spend?

Our position:
- If Sandbar is Seller-related, treat the renewals as **leakage** (locked box) or as a debt-like or working capital adjustment.
- If they were entered after the sale process began, they should have needed Buyer consent under the pre-Completion conduct covenants.
- Otherwise, require a specific indemnity or price reduction for any amount not commercially justified.

**3.14 Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"**

Reject this.
- **Tax:** a standalone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, including tax on the bonuses and any payroll tax or super shortfall. It should be capped at 100% of price, sit outside thresholds, and run for the tax limitation periods described above.
- **IP:** for a SaaS target, IP ownership and non-infringement warranties should at least have a higher cap and a longer period than general warranties. The Ironquay issue shows why.

**3.15 Title (DD-012; DL 10)**

The share register alone is not sufficient evidence of title. The Disclosure Letter itself notes that it "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification."

Our position:
- Title warranties as fundamental warranties (see 3.4), covering no encumbrances, options or other rights over shares.
- Verify against ASIC records, the constitution, any shareholders' agreement (pre-emption waivers), PPSR searches against the Company and the Seller, and historical share issue and transfer documentation.
- Completion deliverables: signed share transfer forms, share certificates (or lost certificate indemnities), board approvals, waivers, director resignations and releases.

**3.16 Office lease (DD-007; DL 7) and Mossvale (DD-009; DL 9)**

These are likely lower risk, but both Disclosure Letter statements are carefully worded ("does not describe it as…," "does not state…"). We should verify them ourselves.
- Confirm that the lease requires notification only and not consent. Put the notice into the completion steps.
- Confirm that the Mossvale restriction on assignment has no change-of-control or deemed-assignment limb.

## 4. Recommendations summary

**Reject outright**
1. Title and capacity warranties under the general cap and time limits. These must be capped at 100% of price, sit outside thresholds, and run for 6–7 years.
2. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature." Carve out fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, indemnities, covenants, leakage and price mechanics.
3. The "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated" default.
4. Constructive, adviser or "discoverable" buyer knowledge. Seek pro-sandbagging, with a fallback to actual knowledge of named individuals.
5. General data-room and public-records disclosure. Seek specific, fair disclosure only, delete "or referred to in," and ensure no cure by bring-down disclosure.
6. The post-Completion Riverlark release.
7. The "settled" status of tax and IP under the general regime.

**Restructure as conditions precedent or Completion deliverables**
8. An unconditional Bluefen consent, with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, waivable by the Buyer only, and best endeavours on the Seller.
9. The Riverlark payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges at Completion.
10. The Ironquay confirmatory assignment, with SOW3 fees paid or deducted.
11. A complete DD-006 incident file and NDB assessment before signing or Completion.

**Price and funds flow**
12. Deduct Riverlark (full payoff amount), the bonuses plus on-costs, and any unpaid Ironquay fees as Debt. Investigate Sandbar as possible leakage or a debt-like item.
13. Add a retention or escrow sized to the DD-006 and Bluefen exposures, or obtain W&I cover with these matters handled outside the policy, since W&I will typically exclude known issues.

**Specific indemnities**, outside the cap, thresholds, disclosure and knowledge
14. DD-006 privacy incident.
15. Ironquay IP, covering ownership and infringement and not just the payment.
16. Pre-Completion tax, including on the bonuses.
17. Undisclosed change-of-control or transaction payments.
18. Sandbar, if it is not resolved through price.

**Negotiable, with suggested positions**
19. General cap: 30–50% without W&I, or around 20% plus W&I.
20. Tipping basket of about 1%. De minimis around AUD 10k with aggregation of related claims.
21. General claims period of 24 months.

**Information requests**
- Confirm internally whether any principal "settled" these points.
- Bluefen: the cl 11.3 text, any termination-for-convenience right, and the status of the approach to Bluefen.
- Riverlark: a draft payoff letter and break costs.
- Ironquay: a full SOW3 fee ledger and confirmation of what IP is embedded in the current product.
- DD-005: the bonus terms and their tax and super treatment.
- DD-006: the forensic report, NDB assessment and notifications.
- Sandbar: whether it is related to Harbourglass, contract dates, terms and termination rights.
- Title: ASIC and PPSR searches and the shareholders' agreement.
- An updated data room index, given the data room cut-off was 22 September.

*These positions should be confirmed with NSW-qualified transaction, tax and privacy counsel before the mark-up goes out. I can prepare a clause-by-clause mark-up or an issues list in the Seller's numbering if that would help.*
